query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Near‐equiatomic, multi‐element nanoparticles that maximize configurational entropy will exhibit enhanced structural and chemical stability under high‐temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions because the high entropy raises diffusion barriers that delay phase segregation and elemental rearrangement.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles with a uniform, single‐phase structure as produced by conventional physical or chemical synthesis methods.
generation.intervention: Synthesize two series of nanoparticles: one with a strictly near‐equiatomic composition (maximizing configurational entropy) and a control series with a slight, intentional deviation from equiatomic ratios.
generation.conditions: Expose the nanoparticles to high-temperature service regimes typical for catalysis (773–1173 K) and thermoelectrics (473–1923 K) in an inert atmosphere to minimize oxidative effects.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniformly distorted lattice stabilized by high configurational entropy, which elevates atomic diffusion energy barriers.
generation.mechanism: High configururational entropy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for atomic diffusion; this suppression of diffusion hinders phase separation and surface segregation under thermal cycling, thereby maintaining the single-phase, chemically homogeneous structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under prolonged high-temperature exposure, the near‐equiatomic (high-entropy) nanoparticles will retain their single-phase structure with minimal signs of phase segregation or elemental clustering, whereas nanoparticles with off‐equiatomic compositions will show increased evidence of phase separation and chemical inhomogeneity.
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized nanoparticles initially verified by X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy as uniform, single-phase solid solutions at room temperature.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to near‐equiatomic, multi‐element nanoparticles produced via standard synthesis routes and tested under inert atmospheres; results may differ if strong oxidative environments or compositions far from equiatomic dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of small deviations from equiatomic composition on diffusion barriers and long-term stability remains to be fully established, and slight residual oxygen in the environment may also influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles as described (near‐equiatomic vs. off‐equiatomic). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature exposure for durations representative of catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions in an inert atmosphere. Monitor the evolution of their phase structure and elemental distribution over time.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase purity and detection of secondary phases
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for identifying microstructural changes or phase separation
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for mapping elemental distributions and segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the near‐equiatomic (high-entropy) nanoparticles do not remain significantly more stable (i.e., showing no less phase segregation or elemental inhomogeneity) than the off‐equiatomic control under the same high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy governs the enhanced stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. In recent years, many researchers have reported that HEA nanoparticles (NPs) having sizes on the nanometer scale (that is, in the range of 1 to 100 nm) show promise with regard to catalytic applications. However, the oxygen chemical potential, μO, exerts a profound influence on the phase stability of Mn2O3 and Fe2O3 compared to that of MnO and FeO. This μO can be tuned by controlling experimental variables such as temperature, T, and oxygen partial pressure, PO2. Recently, we demonstrated that the consideration of PO2 in our calculations was necessary for understanding the formability of entropy stabilized pyrochlore structures (). In this work, we estimate the phase stability of Fe- and Mn-containing oxides in relation to their stable forms, as a function of T and PO2. The formation abilities of FCOs containing Mn and Fe are re-evaluated using MnO and FeO as the reference oxides. These formation abilities will be valid under the experimental conditions where MnO and FeO are more stable than Mn2O3 and Fe2O3. We find that the formation abilities of FCOs containing Mn and Fe are markedly different, compliant with the stability of their reference oxides. Therefore, we predict that several different HEOs can potentially be synthesized in pure rocksalt structures under low oxygen partial pressure.

drafts.hypothesis: The high configurational entropy inherent in near‐equiatomic, multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles is the key factor that preserves their structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions. This entropy stabilizes the single-phase solid solution and retards atomic diffusion that otherwise would lead to phase segregation, even when noble metal content is low.
drafts.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized via standard fabrication approaches with low noble-metal content.
drafts.intervention: Prepare two series of nanoparticles: one with a strictly near-equiatomic composition (high configurational entropy) and a second series with a small intentional deviation from equiatomic ratios (lower configurational entropy), while keeping all other synthesis parameters constant.
drafts.conditions: Expose both nanoparticle series to service regimes representative of catalytic operation (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric use (473–1923 K) in an inert atmosphere to minimize oxidative effects.
drafts.structural_mediator: A uniformly distorted lattice that limits atomic mobility and prevents the nucleation and growth of secondary phases.
drafts.mechanism: High configurational entropy increases the entropy term in the free energy, thus lowering the thermodynamic driving force for phase segregation and atomic diffusion. This effect, in combination with a uniform lattice distortion, inhibits localized elemental diffusion that could otherwise lead to structural reordering or phase separation under high-temperature conditions—even in systems with low noble metal content.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under thermal cycling, the near-equiatomic (high-entropy) nanoparticles are expected to maintain a single-phase structure with minimal signs of phase segregation and stable lattice parameters, as confirmed by techniques such as X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy, whereas the off-equiatomic (lower-entropy) nanoparticles should show measurable phase separation or structural degradation.
drafts.baseline: The initial room-temperature structure and composition of the as-synthesized nanoparticles—verified to be a uniform, single-phase solid solution in the near-equiatomic series.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable only to nanoparticles produced via comparable synthesis routes and having similar size distributions; behavior may differ in bulk materials, markedly different particle sizes, or in reactive environments (e.g., high oxygen partial pressures) where oxidation processes might compete with the entropy-driven stabilization.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one strictly near-equiatomic and one with a deliberately perturbed (off-equiatomic) composition. Subject both sets to extended thermal cycling under catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) conditions in an inert atmosphere. Compare structural integrity and phase purity via X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS).
measurements: XRD to monitor phase composition and lattice parameter shifts
TEM imaging to observe microstructural changes and any phase segregated regions
EDS mapping to detect elemental distributions and clustering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the near-equiatomic (high-entropy) nanoparticles display similar or greater levels of phase segregation, structural rearrangement, or elemental diffusion compared to the off-equiatomic (lower-entropy) nanoparticles under identical thermal conditions, then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy is the primary factor governing structural stability is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The stability of near‐equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles at high temperatures is governed by the magnitude of atomic size mismatch among the constituent elements. Nanoparticles with low size mismatch maintain a homogeneous solid solution under catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions, whereas those with a higher mismatch experience enhanced lattice strain that speeds up diffusion‐mediated phase separation and surface segregation.
drafts.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles fabricated by physical and chemical methods, initially homogeneous in phase and composition.
drafts.intervention: Systematically vary the atomic size mismatch by synthesizing two series of nanoparticles: one with constituent elements having minimal differences in atomic radii (low mismatch) and one with elements that have larger differences in atomic sizes (high mismatch), while keeping the overall near-equiatomic composition fixed.
drafts.conditions: Exposing the nanoparticles to service regime temperatures typical for catalytic operation (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric use (473–1923 K).
drafts.structural_mediator: Local lattice strain induced by atomic size mismatch, which mediates the activation energy for atomic diffusion and phase boundary formation.
drafts.mechanism: High lattice strain provides a driving force for atomic diffusion under service temperatures, resulting in the nucleation of secondary phases or elemental segregation, particularly at surfaces. Conversely, nanoparticles with low atomic size mismatch experience reduced lattice strain, thus suppressing diffusion and maintaining the homogeneous solid-solution structure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with low atomic size mismatch will retain a uniform, single-phase structure under high temperature conditions. In contrast, nanoparticles with high atomic size mismatch will show signatures of phase separation, such as secondary phase formation or elemental segregation (detectable via compositional mapping), especially under prolonged high-temperature exposure.
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized with moderate atomic size mismatch that have been observed to exhibit partial stability, against which the low and high mismatch regimes can be compared.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles with near-equiatomic compositions fabricated by commonly used physical and chemical methods. It may not hold for compositions far from equiatomic ratios or for synthesis routes that introduce controlled defects that alter diffusion pathways. Additionally, extreme temperature conditions beyond the service regimes could invoke melting or other transitions unrelated solely to size mismatch effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of near-equiatomic nanoparticles: one with low atomic size mismatch and one with high atomic size mismatch by selecting appropriate elemental combinations. Subject both series to identical high-temperature environments representative of catalytic (e.g., 1173 K) and thermoelectric (e.g., 1923 K) conditions. Monitor the structural evolution in real time using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) for compositional mapping.
measurements: High-resolution imaging to track phase separation or particle coarsening
XRD patterns to detect emergence of secondary phases
EDX mapping to identify elemental segregation at surfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with high atomic size mismatch do not show significantly greater phase separation or elemental segregation compared to those with low mismatch under identical high-temperature conditions, then the mechanistic role of atomic size mismatch in governing stability would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Under catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions, the preservation of a single-phase, near-equiatomic high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticle is governed by its intrinsic lattice strain—arising from high configurational entropy—that creates large energy barriers to atomic diffusion and phase segregation. This barrier is effective only when the ambient oxygen chemical potential is maintained below a critical threshold, because high oxygen partial pressure can lower the effective diffusion barrier by promoting oxidation and subsequent phase separation.
drafts.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic, single-phase HEA nanoparticles with a high degree of chemical disorder and significant intrinsic lattice strain, optionally featuring thin surface layers (e.g., graphene or oxide passivation) from synthesis.
drafts.intervention: Systematically vary the ambient oxygen partial pressure during high-temperature exposure (within catalytic or thermoelectric regimes) while keeping the nanoparticle composition and size constant.
drafts.conditions: Test conditions should simulate service regimes (e.g., 773–1173 K for catalysis or 473–1923 K for thermoelectrics) with controlled oxygen partial pressures ranging from very low (reducing atmosphere) to moderately high (oxidizing atmosphere).
drafts.structural_mediator: Intrinsic lattice strain induced by compositional disorder in the HEA, which sets high diffusion energy barriers; modulated by the presence or absence of surface passivating layers that may further hinder atomic mobility.
drafts.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of the HEA produces significant lattice distortion, which raises the activation energy for atomic diffusion and thereby inhibits phase segregation and oxidation. However, at elevated oxygen chemical potentials, oxidation processes can overcome these barriers, leading to surface oxidation, atomic rearrangement, and eventual loss of the desirable single-phase structure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles exposed to lower oxygen partial pressures will retain their single-phase, disordered structure and high lattice strain, whereas those subjected to higher oxygen partial pressures will exhibit signs of oxidation (e.g., formation of oxide phases) and phase segregation, observable as changes in crystallography and chemical composition.
drafts.baseline: HEA nanoparticles synthesized and initially characterized under standard ambient conditions with a typical oxygen partial pressure, showing a uniform single-phase structure.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for HEA nanoparticles with near-equiatomic compositions and sufficiently small sizes (nanoscale) where the high-entropy effect dominates, and for service temperatures in the range 473–1923 K. It may not hold if additional passivation features or compositional gradients (beyond near-equiatomic ratios) dominate the diffusion dynamics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a batch of near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles with confirmed single-phase structure. Divide the batch into several groups and expose each group to high-temperature conditions within the target operational range (e.g., 900 K) under controlled atmospheres with incrementally increasing oxygen partial pressures (from reducing to moderately oxidizing). After exposure for a fixed duration, rapidly quench the samples to freeze the microstructure.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect phase segregation or emergence of oxide phases
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) to observe structural integrity and any morphological changes
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to quantify oxidation states and surface chemical composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no systematic increase in oxidation or phase segregation is observed with higher oxygen partial pressures—i.e., if the nanoparticles retain their initial single-phase structure regardless of increased oxygen chemical potential—then the hypothesis that intrinsic lattice strain mediated by configurational entropy is the dominant factor protecting structural and chemical stability under service conditions is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Nanoparticles that are synthesized to maximize uniform severe lattice distortion (through rapid, controlled reduction and thermal shock processing) will better preserve their single‐phase structure and chemical homogeneity under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service regimes because the associated high configurational entropy, together with kinetically induced diffusion barriers from lattice strain, impedes elemental segregation and phase transformation.
drafts.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic, single-phase high-entropy (or complex concentrated) alloy nanoparticles exhibiting severe lattice distortion and a uniform elemental distribution as achieved by rapid synthesis methods.
drafts.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one via a rapid reduction/thermal shock method designed to maximize lattice strain and kinetic barriers, and a control set via a slower reduction process that produces lower levels of lattice distortion.
drafts.conditions: Exposure of both nanoparticle sets to service conditions for catalytic operations (773–1173 K) or thermoelectric applications (473–1923 K) under inert or controlled reactive atmospheres.
drafts.structural_mediator: The degree of lattice distortion and high defect density acting as atomic diffusion barriers.
drafts.mechanism: High configurational entropy favors a disordered, single-phase solid-solution state. When combined with severe lattice distortion, local diffusion energy barriers are increased, thereby kinetically stabilizing the nanoparticle structure by reducing atomic mobility that could otherwise lead to phase segregation during high-temperature operation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles synthesized with high lattice distortion will display significantly less elemental segregation, phase transformation, or compositional inhomogeneity after prolonged high-temperature exposure compared to those made via slower, less-strained synthesis routes.
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles produced with conventional slower reduction methods that yield lower lattice distortion, which are predicted to show increased phase separation or chemical instability under identical high-temperature conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to near-equiatomic, multi-element nanoparticles where the size mismatch among constituent elements is sufficient to induce large strain fields. Its validity may be limited for systems where either the elemental size differences are minimal or where external factors (e.g., oxidative environments) dominate phase behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two groups of HEA nanoparticles using the two described methods (rapid thermal shock versus slower reduction). Subject both groups to identical high-temperature exposure relevant for catalytic/thermoelectric operation. Use ex situ and in situ techniques (e.g., XRD, HRTEM, and elemental mapping) to assess phase purity and elemental distribution before and after thermal treatment.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to monitor changes in phase structure and possible peak broadening or splitting indicating segregation.
High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to assess nanoscale compositional uniformity.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) for surface chemical state analysis pre- and post-thermal exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles synthesized with high lattice distortion do not show statistically significant improvements in preserving single-phase, uniform composition after thermal exposure compared to the control sample, or if both samples exhibit comparable levels of phase segregation and compositional changes, the hypothesis is falsified.
